extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, proofreaders, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for punctuation, quotation, parentheses/brackets, spacing, and comma usage in manuscript and typeset prose according to The Chicago Manual of Style (chapter on Punctuation). Intended to guide consistent punctuation and typographic decisions in editing and publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses/brackets font matching when on own line
rubrics_metrics.description: When a phrase in parentheses or brackets appears on a line by itself, the parentheses or brackets are usually in the same font as the phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to typesetting and font choices; see related guidance for quotation marks and isolated lines (see 13.62).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks font matching to surrounding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should appear in the same font—roman or italic—as the surrounding text, which may or may not match that of the material they enclose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quotation marks are roman in normal text; if the entire title is italic, the surrounding quotation marks may be italicized as part of the title. If a quoted sentence stands alone on a line, quotation marks are usually in same font as the sentence. See also guidance on punctuation relative to quotation marks (6.62+).

rubrics_metrics.name: One space between sentences in typeset matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In typeset matter, one space, not two, should be used between two sentences—whether the first ends in a period, a question mark, an exclamation point, or a closing quotation mark or parenthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the same token, one space, not two, should follow a colon. If a particular design layout calls for more specific spacing between elements (e.g., figure number and caption), design should specify exact amount (em space). See 6.119-21 for related rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation with URLs and email addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences that include an email address or a URL should be punctuated normally; readers should assume any punctuation at the end belongs to the sentence rather than the address/URL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angle brackets or other wrappers are unnecessary in normal prose. Hypertext markup for electronic formats should exclude surrounding punctuation. For dividing an email address or URL at line end, see 7.46. Examples given: Chicago’s forum at http://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org; grammar88@parsed-out.edu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods and commas precede closing quotation marks (traditional US style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods and commas precede closing quotation marks, whether double or single (traditional U.S. style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tradition predates the manual's first edition. Exceptions exist (see 7.79). See table 6.1 for punctuation relative to closing quotation marks and parentheses/brackets. Examples: He described what he heard as a “short, sharp shock.” “Thus conscience does make cowards of us all,” she replied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation relative to closing quotation marks and parentheses/brackets (table)
rubrics_metrics.description: General positions: period and comma inside; semicolon and colon outside; question/exclamation inside or outside depending; em dash inside or outside depending (see specific sections). Parentheses/brackets: period inside if entire sentence enclosed, otherwise inside or outside as noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to table 6.1 and cross-references 6.9, 6.70, 6.74, 6.18, 6.98, 6.101, 6.103 for specifics and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: British (alternative) quotation punctuation system
rubrics_metrics.description: In British style (New Oxford Style Manual), single quotation marks are used and only punctuation marks that appeared in the original material are included within the quotation marks; all others follow the closing quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions are widespread (e.g., periods often placed inside quotes that form complete sentences). Double quotes reserved for quotations within quotations. This system may be appropriate in textual criticism, coding, and technical/scientific settings. See 13.7-8, 13.30-31 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colons/semicolons follow closing quotation marks; question/exclamation placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Colons and semicolons follow closing quotation marks; question marks and exclamation points follow closing quotation marks unless they belong within the quoted matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows the logical rule sometimes absent in traditional US style. Examples illustrate when question/exclamation belong inside or outside. See table 6.1 and sections 6.10, 6.70, 6.74.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space between adjacent single and double quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When single quotation marks are nested within double quotation marks and two marks appear next to each other, a space between the two marks, though not strictly required, aids legibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For print, typesetters may place a thinspace or hair space; in electronic environments, a nonbreaking space prevents the second mark from moving to a new line. Example: “Admit it,” she said. “You haven’t read ‘The Simple Art of Murder.’” See 6.120, 13.30.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the period (definition and spacing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A period marks the end of a declarative or an imperative sentence; between sentences it is followed by a single space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called dot or point in some contexts; British usage calls it a full stop. A period may follow a standalone word or phrase. See index for other uses; cross-reference 2.9, 6.7, 6.119.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods with parentheses and brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: When an entire independent sentence is enclosed in parentheses or square brackets, the period belongs inside the closing parenthesis or bracket; when such material is included within another sentence, the period belongs outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid enclosing more than one complete sentence within another sentence. If an abbreviation ending in a period falls at sentence end, do not add another period (see 6.123 and 6.13). Examples illustrate placement and note where two periods are required (abbrev plus sentence-final).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to omit a terminal period
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place a period after a display line (chapter title, subhead, running head, column head), a phrase used as a caption (with exceptions), a dateline in correspondence, a signature, or an address—unless the expression normally requires a period (e.g., an abbreviation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run-in subheads are followed by a period (see 1.56). Some aesthetic comma omissions at end of display lines may be acceptable (see 8.165). See 6.127-32 for lists and outline style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods in ellipses usage
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis (three periods) may indicate an omission in quoted material or faltering speech/incomplete sentence or thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See detailed rules for ellipses in quotations 13.50-58 and for faltering speech 13.41, 13.55. For other languages and the use of em dash for interruption, see specified sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: General use of the comma
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma indicates the smallest break in sentence structure and usually denotes a slight pause, but logical considerations come first; effective use involves judgment to promote ease of reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical uses exist in scientific and bibliographical contexts. Follow logical rules and cross-references throughout chapter 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas in pairs (set-off elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comma is placed before an element to set it off, a second comma is required if the sentence continues beyond the element being set off (commas in pairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to many comma usages (dates, place-names, parenthetical elements). Exception: commas within titles are considered independent (not treated as set-off). Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement relative to parentheses and brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: When the context calls for a comma at the end of material in parentheses or brackets, the comma should follow the closing parenthesis or bracket; a comma never precedes a closing parenthesis (rare editorial exceptions exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rare cases: a comma may appear inside and immediately before a closing bracket as part of editorial interpolation (see 13.59). Examples show correct placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial (Oxford) comma recommended
rubrics_metrics.description: Items in a series are normally separated by commas; when a conjunction joins the last two elements in a series of three or more, a comma (the serial or Oxford comma) should appear before the conjunction—Chicago strongly recommends this usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents ambiguity; if the last element consists of a pair joined by 'and', the pair should still be preceded by a serial comma and the first 'and'. If serial comma fails to prevent ambiguity, reword. If sentence continues beyond the series, add comma only if required by syntax. See examples and exceptions (6.60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting serial comma before ampersands
rubrics_metrics.description: When an ampersand is used instead of 'and' (e.g., in company names), the serial comma is omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Winken, Blinken & Nod.' See also 14.88, 14.135.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with independent clauses joined by coordinating conjunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When independent clauses are joined by coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, so, yet, etc.), a comma usually precedes the conjunction; for very short closely connected clauses the comma may be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies equally to imperative sentences where subject 'you' is omitted. If clauses are part of a series, follow series rules. For semicolon alternative, see 6.56.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with compound predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma is not normally used to separate a two-part compound predicate joined by a coordinating conjunction (shared subject), though a comma may be needed to prevent misreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show when comma is omitted and when included for clarity. Compound predicates of three or more parts treated as a series are punctuated accordingly (see 6.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'then' when shorthand for 'and then'
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'then' is used as shorthand for 'and then', a comma usually precedes the adverb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare: 'She filled in the last square ... , then yawned.' vs 'She filled in ... and then yawned.' See 6.24 and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with introductory dependent clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a dependent clause precedes the main independent clause, it should be followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent clauses are often introduced by subordinating conjunctions such as if, because, when. Examples: 'If you accept our conditions, we shall agree to the proposal.' Compare with dependent clauses following main clause (6.25-6.27).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with dependent clauses following main clause (restrictive vs nonrestrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent clause following a main clause should not be preceded by a comma if it is restrictive (essential); if the clause is supplementary/nonrestrictive, it should be preceded by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctions can be tenuous; when in doubt rephrase. Examples demonstrate meaning change depending on comma presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with intervening dependent clauses (adjacent conjunctions 'and if' etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a dependent clause intervenes between two clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction, causing 'and if' or similar to appear, the conjunctions need not be separated by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Burton examined the documents for over an hour, and if Smedley had not intervened, the forgery would have been revealed.' A comma would not be wrong; choice may depend on emphasis. See also 6.22, 6.24, 6.26.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with relative clauses: 'that' vs 'which' (restrictive vs nonrestrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictive relative clauses (essential) are usually introduced by 'that' (or who/whom/whose) and are never set off by commas; nonrestrictive clauses (nonessential) are usually introduced by 'which' (or who/whom/whose) and are set off by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although British usage may substitute 'which' for 'that' in restrictive clauses, many writers preserve the distinction. Examples illustrate usage; see 5.250 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with appositives (restrictive vs nonrestrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appositive providing nonessential explanatory information is normally set off by commas; a restrictive appositive providing essential identification is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This year’s poet laureate, K. Lester, spoke first.' vs 'O’Neill’s play The Hairy Ape...' Avoid possessive constructions with nonrestrictive appositives; reword instead. See 5.23, 6.27.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with descriptive phrases (restrictive vs nonrestrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A descriptive phrase that is restrictive (essential) should not be set off by commas; a nonrestrictive descriptive phrase should be enclosed in commas (or preceded by a comma if final).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrast 'The woman with the guitar over her shoulder is my mother.' vs 'My mother, with her guitar over her shoulder, turned to the drummer...' See 6.27.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with participial phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: An introductory participial phrase is normally set off from the rest of the sentence by a comma. When such a phrase occurs mid-sentence, set it off by commas unless it is restrictive (provides essential information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Exhilarated by her morning workout, she headed for the ocean.' vs 'Actors forgetting their lines may be forced to ad-lib.' Also, when participial modifies subject via linking verb, do not use a comma (see 5.101). See examples for end-of-sentence placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with adverbial phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: An introductory adverbial phrase can usually be followed by a comma but need not be unless misreading is likely; shorter phrases less likely to require a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in middle of sentence, adverbial phrases are normally set off by commas. At the end of a sentence, a comma is necessary only when phrase is nonrestrictive. Examples illustrate choices and when not to use comma (inverted sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with participial/adverbial phrase plus conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a participial or adverbial phrase immediately follows a coordinating conjunction, comma usage depends on whether the conjunction joins two independent sentences; if it is part of the predicate or joins a compound predicate, the first comma follows the conjunction; if it joins independent clauses the comma precedes the conjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'We were extremely tired and, in light of our binge..., anxious to go home.' vs 'We were elated, but realizing that the day was almost over, we decided to go to bed.' Adding a second comma after 'but' would be acceptable for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with introductory words ('yes', 'no', 'OK', 'well')
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma should follow an introductory 'yes', 'no', 'OK', 'well', and the like, except in certain informal or dialog cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Yes, it is true...' 'No, neither scenario...' 'OK, I'll try...' Exceptions: 'No you will not!' as informal/dialect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with introductory 'oh' or 'ah'
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma usually follows an exclamatory 'oh' or 'ah' unless followed by an exclamation mark (or dash) or forms part of a phrase (e.g., 'oh boy'). No comma follows a vocative 'O' or archaic poetic 'O'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Oh, you're right!' 'Ah, here we are at last!' 'Oh mighty king!' See also 7.31.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with two or more adjectives preceding a noun (coordinate adjectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple adjectives preceding a noun can be joined by 'and' (coordinate adjectives) and reversed in order without changing meaning, separate them with commas; if adjectives form a unit with the noun (not coordinate), do not use commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a faithful, sincere friend' vs 'inexpensive quartz watch.' For repeated adjectives, place comma between repeats (e.g., 'Many, many people'). See 5.91.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with dates (month-day-year) and addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: In month-day-year style, commas must set off the year and separate elements like day-of-week from month/day; in day-month-year (British) no commas needed around year. Commas set off elements in addresses or place-names run into text; mailing address punctuation should be minimal and follow postal conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'February 2, 2006, at the State Theatre' and 'Monday, May 5, was a holiday.' For ISO and year-month-day styles see 9.36. Institutional names containing place-names require second comma when appearing mid-clause (e.g., 'California State University, Northridge,'). See 6.81 and postal guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with quotations introduced by said/replied/etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent clause quoted as dialogue or from text and introduced with verbs like said, replied, asked, wrote is usually introduced with a comma; this applies regardless of explanatory text position relative to the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'She replied,

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with quoted or italicized titles and expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles or expressions set off with quotation marks or italics are usually treated like noun forms; commas are used or omitted as they would be with any other noun, and appositive rules determine comma use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting an unnecessary comma before a title following a noun unless it is nonrestrictive. Examples illustrate restrictive vs nonrestrictive treatment of titles; see 8.163 and 7.62 for quote vs italics rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with direct questions included within sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct question included within a sentence but not enclosed in quotation marks is usually introduced by a comma and begins with a capital letter; if the question ends before the end of the sentence, no comma is required after the question mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'She wondered, What am I doing?' If awkward, rephrase as an indirect question (no comma, no question mark, not capitalized): 'She wondered what she was doing.' See 6.69 and 6.125.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas in personal names with generational suffixes (Jr., Sr., III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas are not required with Jr. and Sr., and they are never used to set off Jr., III, etc., when used as part of a name; in an inverted name (index), a comma is required before such an element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'John Doe Sr.' vs 'Doe, John, Sr.' If a comma is used to set off Jr. or Sr. in a sentence, a second comma is normally required (commas in pairs); rephrase to avoid possessive awkwardness.
